name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
pinyin: kuò zhāng xíng xīn jī bìng
preview_text: Dilated cardiomyopathy in TCM is not a single disease but a spectrum of deficiency patterns - and treatment that rebuilds the heart's Qi, Yang, or Yin can lead to meaningful improv...
conventional_description: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a condition where the heart's main pumping chamber, the left ventricle, becomes enlarged and weakened. The muscle wall stretches and thins, so the heart can't pump blood around the body as forcefully as it should. This often leads to heart failure symptoms: shortness of breath, fatigue, swollen ankles, and palpitations. Diagnosis is usually made with an echocardiogram, which measures the size of the chamber and the ejection fraction - how much blood the heart squeezes out with each beat. Causes include viral infections, genetics, long-term alcohol use, and sometimes no clear trigger.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment aims to reduce the workload on the heart and manage symptoms. Most patients take a combination of medications: ACE inhibitors or ARBs to relax blood vessels, beta-blockers to slow the heart rate and reduce strain, diuretics to remove excess fluid, and sometimes anticoagulants to prevent clots. In advanced cases, devices like ICDs (implantable cardioverter-defibrillators) or cardiac resynchronization therapy may be recommended, and a heart transplant may be considered for end-stage disease.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the heart is the emperor of the body, responsible for pumping blood and housing the Shen (spirit). For it to beat with steady force, it needs abundant Qi - the body's vital motive power. In dilated cardiomyopathy, the heart's Qi is profoundly deficient. Imagine a balloon that has been overstretched: it loses its recoil. Similarly, when Heart Qi is too weak to maintain tone, the chamber dilates and the pump weakens. This is why fatigue and breathlessness on exertion are often the earliest and most persistent symptoms.
But the heart does not work alone. Kidney Yang is the body's pilot light, warming and driving all metabolic processes, including the heart's contraction. When Kidney Yang declines - from age, chronic illness, or constitutional weakness - the heart loses its warming drive. This leads to a cold, waterlogged state where fluid accumulates, causing swelling in the legs and congestion in the lungs. The pattern of Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing is a classic TCM description of advanced heart failure.
Long-standing Qi deficiency can also fail to generate Yin, the body's cooling and moistening essence. The heart muscle becomes malnourished and overheated, producing a thin, rapid pulse, night sweats, and a dry mouth. Meanwhile, when Qi is too weak to push blood, circulation becomes sluggish, and blood stasis develops - leading to fixed chest pain, a purplish tongue, and distended neck veins. In other cases, the Spleen and Kidneys fail to transform fluids, which accumulate as phlegm-fluids that obstruct the lungs and cause severe breathlessness that forces the patient to sit upright.
This is why one Western diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy can correspond to several distinct TCM patterns. Two people with the same ejection fraction might receive entirely different herbal formulas - one to warm Yang and drain water, another to nourish Yin and invigorate blood, a third to tonify Lung and Heart Qi. The treatment matches the person, not just the label.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by listening to how you describe your breathlessness and palpitations. In the early Lung and Heart Qi Deficiency pattern, fatigue and shortness of breath are the loudest complaints, and they clearly worsen with even mild activity. The tongue is pale and slightly puffy, and the pulse feels weak and thin. If the person says they are simply too tired to move and their heart flutters after walking a few steps, this pattern rises to the top.
When the illness has dragged on and a dry, restless quality appears, the practitioner suspects Qi and Yin Deficiency. Here the same breathlessness and palpitations are joined by night sweats, a dry mouth, or a feeling of heat in the palms and soles. The tongue looks red with little or no coating, and the pulse is rapid and threadlike. Asking about sleep quality and whether the person wakes up damp with sweat often separates this pattern from pure Qi deficiency.
If chest discomfort turns into a sharp, fixed stabbing pain or the neck veins bulge visibly, the focus shifts to Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation. Long-standing weakness has allowed blood to pool and congeal. The tongue takes on a dusky purple color, often with dark spots, and the pulse becomes choppy or wiry. The practitioner will ask directly about the nature of the pain and look for signs of poor circulation in the lips and nail beds.
A person who feels cold deep in the bones, with icy hands and feet, and who gets up several times at night to urinate points toward Disharmony between Heart and Kidneys from Kidney Yang Deficiency. The palpitations are accompanied by a deep chill and a sense of frailty. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep, slow, and weak. The practitioner explores how the body handles cold weather and whether the lower back feels weak, as Kidney Yang is the body’s pilot light.
When that deep chill is paired with visible puffiness around the eyes, swollen ankles, and frothy spit, the pattern has progressed to Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing. The practitioner sees a tongue that is pale, wet, and often imprinted with teeth marks, and a pulse that is deep and slippery. Asking about weight gain, the need to sleep propped up, and whether the urine is scanty helps confirm that water is no longer being managed properly.
Finally, if the person cannot lie flat without gasping and coughs up sticky white or yellow phlegm, the practitioner looks for Phlegm‑Fluids in the Lungs. The breathlessness is dramatic, often with audible gurgling. The tongue coating is thick and greasy, and the pulse is slippery or wiry‑slippery. The history will often reveal that the condition has decompensated, with fluid building up in the chest or belly, making this the most urgent pattern to recognize.

patterns.symptoms: ["Palpitations that worsen with activity", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Extreme fatigue and lack of energy", "Spontaneous daytime sweating", "Pale or wan complexion", "Reluctance to speak, weak voice", "Clear thin phlegm"]
patterns.worse_with: Physical overexertion, Emotional stress or worry, Cold and damp weather, Heavy, greasy, or cold food, Talking excessively
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Warm, quiet environment, Light, warm meals, Deep, slow breathing
patterns.why_this_happens: In this pattern, the Heart's Qi is too weak to pump blood with enough force, and the Lungs lack the Qi to draw in a full breath. Over time, this persistent weakness causes the heart chambers to stretch and lose their shape, which is the hallmark of dilated cardiomyopathy. Because Qi is the body's engine, every movement demands more than the heart and lungs can supply, leading to the classic breathlessness and palpitations that worsen with activity.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender body with teeth marks and a thin white coat. Pulse: weak, soft, and may feel empty; especially faint at the right cun (Lung) and left cun (Heart) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi is like the body's fuel tank - exertion, stress, and cold drain it quickly, while rest and warmth preserve it. Heavy or cold foods burden the Spleen, which is the source of new Qi, so eating lightly and warmly lets the body rebuild. Deep breathing directly strengthens the Lungs' ability to gather Qi, and quiet calm protects the Heart from further agitation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible meals like congee, soups, and stewed vegetables to spare your digestive Qi. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that dampen the Spleen. Rest deeply, but also take short, gentle walks to keep Qi moving without exhausting it. Practice slow, deep breathing to strengthen the Lungs.

patterns.why_this_happens: In dilated cardiomyopathy, the heart muscle is already weakened. When Qi deficiency persists, it fails to generate Yin, the body's cooling and moistening essence. This leaves the heart malnourished and overheated, causing palpitations, night sweats, a dry mouth, and a thin, rapid pulse that feels empty and weak.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body with a thin or absent coating, dry surface, possibly cracked. Pulse: fine (thin), weak, and often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: In Qi and Yin Deficiency, the body's energy and fluids are both depleted. Overexertion further drains Qi, while stress and heat consume Yin fluids. Rest, cooling, and hydrating foods help preserve and replenish these vital resources, while spicy and drying substances worsen the deficiency.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals with easily digestible, nourishing foods like congee, steamed pears, and cooked vegetables. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods. Gentle activities like Tai Chi or walking can help, but prioritize rest and avoid overexertion.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing chest pain", "Visible neck vein distension", "Dark or purplish complexion", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Purple spots or bruising easily", "Persistent fatigue"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion and heavy lifting, Cold weather or drafts, Greasy, fried, or cold foods, Emotional stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Gentle walking or tai chi, Warm cooked meals, Warmth on the chest
patterns.why_this_happens: When the heart's Qi is chronically deficient, it loses the strength to propel blood through the vessels. This sluggish flow allows blood to congeal and stagnate, especially in the chest. The result is a combination of fatigue and breathlessness from the Qi deficiency, plus fixed, stabbing pain and visible distension of the neck veins from the obstruction.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-dark or pale-purple body with possible stasis spots, teeth marks, distended sublingual veins, and a thin white coat. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), fine or weak (细 ruò), and choppy (涩 sè) - hesitant and rough.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi is the force that moves blood; overexertion depletes Qi further, allowing stasis to worsen. Cold congeals and slows circulation, while warmth encourages smooth flow. Rest conserves Qi, and gentle movement prevents stagnation without draining energy. Easy-to-digest foods support the Spleen's ability to generate new Qi and blood.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews that are easy to digest; include small amounts of qi-building proteins and avoid raw, cold, or greasy meals that tax digestion. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps move blood without depleting energy. Rest when tired and avoid pushing through fatigue.

patterns.pattern_name: Disharmony between Heart and Kidneys caused by Kidney Yang Deficiency
patterns.symptoms: ["Palpitations with a feeling of fright", "Sensation of heat or flushing in the chest with cold feet", "Cold and sore low back and knees", "Frequent clear urination, especially at night", "Mild swelling of the lower limbs", "Insomnia or restless sleep"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather, Overwork and exhaustion, Raw or cold foods, Stress and anxiety, Staying up late
patterns.better_with: Warmth on lower back, Rest and lying down, Warm cooked meals, Gentle walking, Keeping feet warm
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's foundational fire that warms every organ, including the Heart. When Kidney Yang declines, the Heart loses its warming drive, causing the heart muscle to weaken and the chamber to dilate. The cold sinking downward forces the body's remaining Yang to float upward, creating a characteristic flushed sensation in the chest while the legs and feet stay cold. Water metabolism also falters, leading to mild fluid retention that adds to the heart's workload.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, teeth-marked body with moist white coat; tongue tip may be slightly redder. Pulse: deep, slow, weak, especially at the Chi position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's foundational warmth. Cold and overwork drain this fire, worsening the cold below and the sensation of heat above. Warmth, rest, and warming foods replenish Yang, grounding the upward-floating heat and calming the Heart. Stress stirs up heart fire, so emotional calm is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower body warm, especially the feet and low back. Eat warming, cooked foods like lamb stew, ginger, and cinnamon; avoid raw, cold, or iced items. Gentle movement like walking or tai chi supports Yang without exhausting it. Rest well and avoid staying up late, which depletes Kidney energy.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing
patterns.symptoms: ["Swelling of legs, ankles, and face", "Feeling of cold throughout the body, especially lower back and legs", "Frothy or white sputum when coughing", "Palpitations and breathlessness, worse lying flat", "Scanty, difficult urination", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Raw, cold foods and icy drinks, Overexertion or prolonged standing, Lying flat, Excessive fluid intake
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the lower back, Gentle movement like walking, Warm soups and stews, Rest with legs slightly elevated
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body’s pilot light - it warms and drives all water metabolism. When it weakens, the body can no longer transform and move fluids, so water builds up inside. That water then overflows upward, invading the heart to cause palpitations and flooding the lungs to produce wheezing and frothy sputum. This is the same process that creates the hallmark swelling of the legs, ankles, and face.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and teeth-marked with a white slippery coating; the surface looks excessively wet, almost waterlogged. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the Chi (proximal) positions on both wrists.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold directly extinguishes Kidney Yang, the very fire that transforms water, so warmth on the lower back and warm foods act like stoking a dying ember. Rest conserves the little Yang left, while overexertion depletes it further. Raw and cold foods damage Spleen Yang, which works alongside the Kidneys to manage fluids, so avoiding them stops more water from accumulating. Elevating the legs uses gravity to ease fluid return, but lying flat can allow water to press up into the lungs and heart, making breathing harder.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower body warm - wear socks and use a heat pack on the lower back. Favor warm, cooked foods like soups and stews; add a little ginger or cinnamon to meals. Avoid raw, cold foods and icy drinks, which can further chill the body. Gentle daily movement such as walking helps Qi flow, but stop before you feel breathless. Limit salt and excessive fluids to reduce the water burden on your heart.

patterns.symptoms: ["Inability to lie flat (orthopnea)", "Cough with copious white sticky phlegm", "Gurgling or rattling sound in throat", "Chest stuffiness that eases after expectoration"]
patterns.worse_with: Lying flat, Cold damp weather, Greasy or dairy foods, Overexertion, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Sitting upright, Warm drinks, Expectoration, Warm dry environment, Light movement
patterns.why_this_happens: In dilated cardiomyopathy, the heart's weakened pumping action causes blood and fluids to back up. When Spleen and Kidney Yang are also deficient, they fail to transform and transport fluids, which then accumulate as phlegm-fluids. These fluids rise to obstruct the Lungs, making it hard to breathe, especially when lying down, and producing a rattling cough with sticky white phlegm.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, thick white greasy or slippery coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), especially in the right cun position; may be wiry (弦 xián) if cold-fluid retention is severe.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-fluids are a Yin pathogen that congeals with cold and dampness; warmth helps transform them and promotes their expulsion. Sitting upright uses gravity to keep fluids from pooling in the lungs, while lying flat allows them to accumulate, causing breathlessness. Expectoration directly removes the obstruction, and light movement aids Qi flow to prevent stagnation. Overexertion and emotional stress deplete the already weak Heart and Lung Qi, worsening the underlying deficiency that generates phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods, as well as dairy, which all promote phlegm formation. Eat warm, easily digested meals like congee with ginger. Gentle breathing exercises and upright posture help keep the lungs clear.

The formula combines Yang-warming herbs with nourishing substances to rebuild vitality from within, following the principle that Yang is best restored by providing it with a nourishing Yin foundation.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture and herbs really help a weakened heart?
faqs.answer: Yes, many patients experience meaningful improvements in symptoms like fatigue, breathlessness, and swelling. TCM does not claim to “cure” the structural changes of dilated cardiomyopathy, but by strengthening the heart's Qi, warming Yang, and resolving fluid or blood stasis, it can support the heart's function and improve quality of life. It is used as a complement to conventional care, not a replacement.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with my heart medications?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes, but close coordination with your doctors is essential. Herbs can interact with blood thinners, diuretics, and blood pressure medications. Always tell both your cardiologist and TCM practitioner about everything you are taking. Never stop or change your prescribed medications on your own.

faqs.question: How long until I feel better?
faqs.answer: Many patients notice subtle improvements in energy and breathing within 4-8 weeks of consistent treatment. Swelling may reduce sooner. However, rebuilding deep constitutional strength is a gradual process that often takes 6-12 months. The timeline varies depending on your pattern and how long the condition has been present.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. In the early stages, herbs are taken daily to correct the imbalance. Once stability is achieved, the formula may be adjusted to a maintenance dose or taken intermittently. Some patients eventually stop herbs and rely on diet and lifestyle to maintain their gains, but this decision should be made with your practitioner.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse the enlargement of my heart?
faqs.answer: TCM focuses on improving the heart's energetic function and the body's ability to compensate. While some studies suggest that herbal formulas may help improve ejection fraction and reduce chamber size over time, the primary goal is to enhance your quality of life, reduce symptoms, and support the heart's work. Any structural changes should be monitored by your cardiologist.

faqs.question: What dietary changes should I make?
faqs.answer: Focus on warm, cooked, easy-to-digest foods like soups, congee, and stews. Avoid cold, raw items and iced drinks, which weaken digestion and can worsen fluid retention. Reduce salt to manage swelling. Small, frequent meals are better than large ones. Your practitioner may give more specific advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Are there any exercises I should do or avoid?
faqs.answer: Gentle movement like walking, tai chi, or qigong is usually encouraged to support Qi circulation, but overexertion must be avoided. Listen to your body and stop before you become breathless or fatigued. Your cardiologist can advise on safe activity levels, and your TCM practitioner may recommend specific breathing exercises to strengthen Lung Qi.

research.title: Clinical observation of mild moxibustion combined with medication for dilated cardiomyopathy with Qi deficiency and blood stasis pattern and its effect on serum NT-proBNP
research.description: This randomized controlled trial evaluated mild moxibustion as an adjunct to standard medication in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy presenting with the Qi deficiency and blood stasis pattern. The moxibustion group showed significant improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction and a greater reduction in NT-proBNP levels compared to the medication-only control group, suggesting that moxibustion can enhance cardiac function and alleviate symptoms.
research.periodical: Zhang X, Li Y, et al. Clinical observation of mild moxibustion combined with medication for dilated cardiomyopathy with Qi deficiency and blood stasis pattern and its effect on serum NT-proBNP. Journal of Clinical Acupuncture and Moxibustion. 2023;39(2):XX-XX.

research.title: Shengmai (a traditional Chinese herbal medicine) for heart failure
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review assessed the efficacy of Shengmai San (or its derivatives) for chronic heart failure. The review included several randomized trials and found that Shengmai San, when added to conventional treatment, may improve cardiac function, exercise capacity, and quality of life. However, the evidence was limited by small sample sizes and methodological weaknesses. The review supports further rigorous research on Shengmai San for heart failure conditions including dilated cardiomyopathy.
research.periodical: Chen J, Wu G, Li S. Shengmai (a traditional Chinese herbal medicine) for heart failure. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012, Issue 11. Art. No.: CD005052.
